An energy declaration (in Swedish “energideklaration”) is an official, standardized report of a building’s energy performance. It serves to inform owners, buyers, tenants and public authorities about how much energy the building uses, how it is constructed and operated, and which measures could improve its efficiency. Key points are:

2. Who Prepares It  
   • A certified energy expert (energiexpert) visits the building, inspects its envelope, heating and ventilation systems, and gathers data on floor area, number of floors, age, construction type, etc.  
   • The inspector may use the building’s technical drawings and utility bills to verify consumption figures.

Each use-category has its own typical occupancy patterns, internal heat gains and ventilation requirements, and thus its own impact on total energy consumption. Below is an overview of the most common premises types and how they influence energy use:

1. Residential Premises  
   – Examples: apartments, single-family dwellings, student rooms.  
   – Energy factors:  
     • Heating and domestic hot water demand driven by occupant behaviour (set-point temperatures, ventilation habits, hot-water use).  
     • Moderate lighting loads, mainly in living spaces.  
     • Electrical appliances (kitchens, laundry) contribute to internal gains.  

2. Office and Administrative Premises  
   – Examples: open-plan offices, meeting rooms, reception areas.  
   – Energy factors:  
     • Extended operating hours (often 8–18), high lighting loads (especially if windowless zones).

In most residential and commercial buildings, electricity consumption is dominated by a handful of end-use categories. While exact shares vary by climate, building type and occupant behaviour, the following are typically the most significant:

1. Space heating and/or domestic hot water (when served by electric boilers or heat pumps)  
   – In electrically heated buildings this can account for 40–70 % of total electricity use.

   – Refrigeration, cooking, laundry, entertainment and IT loads often contribute 15–30 %.

Optimizing natural ventilation in a house involves both architectural design and simple retrofit measures. The goal is to use wind pressure and buoyancy (stack effect) to move fresh air through living spaces without mechanical assistance. Here are the key strategies:

1. Orient and plan openings for cross-ventilation  
   • Place operable windows or vents on opposite or adjacent walls, aligned with prevailing wind directions.  
   • Use large, easily operable windows in the main living areas to maximize airflow when conditions allow.  

2. Exploit the stack (buoyancy) effect  
   • Include high-level vents or small roof-mounted openings (e.g. ridge vents, louvred vents) to let warm air escape.

You won’t find main‐fuse size in the national building register or the EPC data – it’s part of your electrical installation documentation. To determine its capacity:

1. On the distribution board  
   • Open your home’s main electrical cabinet (often in a basement, utility room or by the front door).  
   • Look at the main switch or fuse carrier – the rated current (in amperes, e.g. 16 A, 25 A, 63 A) is printed on the switch/fuse or on a label inside the door.

2. In your electricity network agreement  
   • Your grid operator (local utility) specifies the maximum fuse size you’re allowed under your contract. The agreement or welcome letter will state the contracted fuse rating.

3. In the as-built electrical documentation  
   • If you have handover papers from construction or an electrical inspection report, the main‐fuse rating will be recorded there.

• prevent overloading local grid connections or building electrical installations  
• maximise utilization of existing supply capacity  
• avoid costly network upgrades or punitive tariff peaks

• For normal (day-to-day) lighting, a maintained illuminance of around 100–150 lux measured at floor or tread level is commonly recommended.  
• Some national or industry standards (for example EN 12464-1 for indoor workplaces or local building regulations such as Sweden’s Boverkets byggregler) set a minimum of 100 lux for circulation areas.  
• Emergency lighting standards (e.g. EN 1838) typically require at least 1 lux along the path of escape.  

Because local regulations and the classification of the stairwell (residential, commercial, public) may impose higher or lower requirements, you should always verify the exact figures in the applicable building code or lighting standard for your jurisdiction.

• Heated stairwells (i.e. stairwells that form part of the building’s conditioned volume) should be designed for at least +16 °C.  – Many larger apartment blocks and public buildings in practice maintain +17 to +18 °C in corridors and stairwells for user comfort and to avoid cold bridges and condensation.

Yes. Reducing your indoor temperature is one of the simplest and most cost-effective ways to cut a building’s heating energy use. Every degree you lower the thermostat reduces the temperature difference (ΔT) between inside and outside, and because heat loss through walls, windows and ventilations is roughly proportional to ΔT, you save energy almost immediately.

Key points:
• Typical savings: Turning down the thermostat by 1 °C can reduce heating energy consumption by about 5–7 %.  
• Recommended set-points: Many energy-saving guidelines suggest 19–20 °C for living rooms and 16–18 °C in bedrooms when you’re asleep or away.  
• Night setback and setbacks for unoccupied periods: Dropping the temperature by 3–4 °C overnight or during the day when no one is home can multiply savings without affecting comfort.  
• System considerations: If you have a modern heat-pump or condensing boiler, it will run less often at lower flow temperatures, improving its seasonal efficiency.
